data.title: Star denies OKX theft; Bitcoin's correlation with gold hits record high.
data.description:
Headline

▌OKX Star Denies Claims of Over $2 Billion Stolen from Exchange

On November 28th, OKX founder Star denied claims that over $2 billion had been stolen from OKX, stating that the news was false. He stated that on-chain transactions are publicly verifiable, and facts speak louder than rumors.

▌Bitcoin-Gold Correlation Reaches All-Time High This Year

On November 28th, according to an article published on the X platform by Bitcoin Magazine, data from Galaxy Research shows that the correlation between Bitcoin and gold has reached an all-time high this year. The post also stated that the narrative of "Bitcoin as digital gold" remains active.

▌Chilean Antitrust Authority Seeks $80 Million Fine Against Apple

On November 28, Chile's competition regulator (FNE) filed a request with the country's antitrust court on Friday to fine Apple (AAPL.O) approximately $80 million and order it to take corrective measures, arguing that Apple abused its dominant position in the iOS operating system market. The regulator stated that since at least 2019, the US technology company has restricted competition in app distribution and in-app payments for digital goods on the iOS platform. FNE stated on social media that the sought fine is equivalent to 30% of Apple's sales revenue for product lines and services related to the violations during the investigation period.

Blockchain and AI Applications

▌Telegram Urgently Reminds iPhone Users to Update iOS System Immediately

On November 28th, Telegram issued an urgent reminder to iPhone users to immediately update their iOS version, warning that outdated versions contain security vulnerabilities that would put user data and accounts at risk. It did not disclose details of the vulnerability or how it could be exploited, only urging users to upgrade to the latest system as soon as possible.

▌Scott Aaronson: AI Lab May Announce Major Breakthrough in Cryptoanalysis

On November 28th, computer scientist Scott Aaronson stated that he possesses specific information that an AI lab will soon announce a major breakthrough in theoretical cryptoanalysis, but this breakthrough will not pose an imminent danger to currently deployed cryptographic systems.

▌K33: Recent AI Mathematical Advances Have Not Proved Bitcoin Cryptography Has Been Cracked

On November 28th, K33 researchers stated that recent AI-assisted mathematical advances have not yet proven that Bitcoin's cryptographic system has been cracked. Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge previously proposed a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis using Claude, and related academic reviews are still ongoing. K33 stated that the proof itself does not provide a method for attacking the cryptographic system. Researchers also pointed out that even if P is proven to be equal to NP, theoretically existing algorithms may not be able to be constructed, or their running time may be too long; conversely, even if the two are proven to be unequal, Bitcoin's security cannot be guaranteed, because faster algorithms targeting its cryptographic system may still emerge independently. On November 28th, LayerZero announced over 40 genesis validators for its Zero blockchain, including ARK Invest, Tether, Deutsche Telekom, Broadridge, Gemini, Hashed, Zero Hash, Nansen, and Keyrock, distributed across Asia Pacific, Europe, and North America, covering financial institutions, large enterprises, and digital asset industry companies. These validators will be responsible for validating Zero's blocks and transactions from the very first block. ZRO holders can delegate their tokens to validators for staking, and new validators will join later. LayerZero states that Zero is a high-performance blockchain divided into zones based on use cases, covering scenarios such as transactions and AI Agent payments. The wider distribution of validators reduces the risk of concentration. The Zero mainnet will launch simultaneously with the on-chain transaction engine LayerZero ATLAS on November 30th. ATLAS is deployed at the underlying layer of the trading venue, supporting instant settlement. Initially, its capacity exceeds 250,000 transactions per second. LayerZero claims that in internal testing, it processed approximately 1.5 million orders per second, with a median latency of approximately 850 microseconds.

▌WLFI Sells 12,121 ETH, Expected Loss of $19.26 Million

On November 28th, according to on-chain analyst Ember, WLFI sold 12,121 ETH (approximately $20.06 million) at a loss. Four hours ago, WLFI's strategic reserve wallet sold 12,121 ETH on-chain for 17.58 million USDC and 2.48 million USD1, at a selling price of $1,655. The ETH sold was purchased last year at an average price of approximately $3,244, resulting in a loss of $19.26 million.

▌ CryptoQuant: Bitcoin's Continued Rebound Requires a Resurgence in USDT Supply On November 28th, CryptoQuant research indicated that for Bitcoin to sustain its recovery and rise, increased demand is necessary; historically, sustained rebounds have been accompanied by a resurgence in USDT supply. The research shows that as of November 23rd, the combined USDT supply on Ethereum and Tron was $174.5 billion, a decrease of $12.9 billion from the record high on May 4th, a drop of 6.9%. During periods of USDT supply contraction, Bitcoin's 60-day average return was -9.5%, negative 73% of the time; when supply increased, the corresponding figures were 7.6% and 42%. **Important Economic Developments** On November 28, amid a worsening economic downturn and political and budgetary turmoil ahead of the election, Standard & Poor's (S&P) downgraded France's credit rating outlook to negative. S&P maintained France's "A+" rating, six notches above speculative (junk) grade, placing it on par with countries like Spain and Japan. However, S&P stated that the risk of a future downgrade for France is increasing. In a statement on Friday, S&P said, "The negative outlook for France reflects the continued increase in French government debt and a weak economic growth outlook against a backdrop of weak political consensus and difficulty in reaching an agreement on how to address the massive structural budget deficit." This adjustment means that France now has a negative outlook from all three major rating agencies. Fitch took similar action last month. UBS Recommends Buying Silver on Dips, Expects Significant Rebound in 2027 On November 28th, UBS stated that silver's recent decline has been excessive. The bank pointed out that silver prices have plummeted nearly 70% from their 2026 highs, making this sell-off one of the most severe in decades. UBS strategist Dominic Schneider stated that silver prices have been oversold. Meanwhile, the gold-silver ratio has risen to 88, indicating an improvement in silver's relative valuation. UBS expects the Federal Reserve to end its rate hike cycle in the first quarter of 2027, followed by a gradual decline in inflation and a renewed rise in market expectations for rate cuts. The bank favors a long position in silver in the coming months and anticipates that, due to higher price volatility, silver's rebound could exceed that of gold.

▌AI Boom Boosts US Stocks: S&P 500 Posts Biggest Weekly Gain Since April 2025

On November 28, US stocks ended a turbulent week on Wall Street with gains, as a rebound in artificial intelligence trading accelerated, reducing investor demand for US Treasuries and safe-haven currencies. The renewed AI boom propelled the Nasdaq 100, which had been on the verge of a bear market, up 2.6%. The S&P 500 delivered its strongest weekly performance since April 2025. US stocks closed early the day after Thanksgiving.

... Invesco Increases Strive Holdings by 152,366 Shares in Q3, Up 346% On November 28th, according to a post on the Bitcoin Treasuries platform, asset management company Invesco increased its holdings in Bitcoin treasury company Strive (ASST) by 152,366 shares in the third quarter. Its reported holdings increased by 346% to 196,384 shares, with a quarter-end value of $5.8 million. Can Bitcoin Still Be Called "Digital Gold" Amid Geopolitical Crises? Every time a geopolitical crisis occurs, gold prices rise while Bitcoin prices plummet. After six tests, the claim of "digital gold" has never been substantiated by data. Countries hoard gold but exclude Bitcoin from their reserves. For investors, Bitcoin exhibits an asymmetry: it falls with stocks but doesn't rise with them. Three structural asymmetries prevent Bitcoin from achieving safe-haven status: an overabundance of derivatives (market structure), the dominance of leveraged traders (participant composition), and a lack of repeatable behavioral records (behavioral accumulation). Bitcoin is not a safe-haven asset, but it is a "crisis-useful asset," capable of functioning when borders are closed and banks fail. If these three asymmetries narrow, Bitcoin may no longer be a replica of gold but a completely new "next-generation gold." Generational shifts and the widespread adoption of algorithms are key factors that could accelerate this process.

data.title: Russia reduces its gold holdings for 10 consecutive months: Tether's buying activity cools down.
data.description:
Russia reduced its gold holdings by approximately 72 tons from January to October, making it the only major seller to consistently sell monthly. Turkey net sold about 70 tons in the first quarter, while Azerbaijan sold 21.9 tons due to exceeding its portfolio limit. Saudi Arabia's financing needs fueled speculation of a gold sell-off, but there is no evidence of large-scale reductions. Tether's total gold holdings increased slightly, but the pace of increase slowed significantly, with purchases of 14 tons in the second quarter almost ceasing recently. The selling pressure in the gold market stems not only from investor profit-taking but also from some official holders continuing to reduce their holdings under financial pressure. According to GoldFix statistics, as of September, the national oil funds of Turkey, Russia, and Azerbaijan collectively net sold approximately 166 tons of gold. Russia was the only holder to sell monthly for ten consecutive months, with its gold holdings declining month by month from January to October, totaling a reduction of approximately 72 tons. The Central Bank of Turkey sold approximately 70 tons of gold in the first quarter, primarily in March, and also used another 80 tons for gold-foreign exchange swaps that month. The Azerbaijan National Oil Fund sold 21.9 tons in the first quarter due to rising gold prices causing its gold holdings to exceed the portfolio limit; its holdings remained unchanged at 178.1 tons for the following six months. Tether, which has been repeatedly mentioned in the market, did not experience a large-scale sell-off. Its USDT reserves decreased by 3.4 tons in September compared to June, but its XAUT token reserves increased by 3.7 tons during the same period, resulting in a slight increase in its combined holdings from 168.2 tons to 168.5 tons.

Russia Continues to Sell Gold, Turkey Focuses on Reduction, Azerbaijan Rebalances at High Prices

The Russian central bank's gold sales mainly occur in the domestic market, driven by the Ministry of Finance using the National Wealth Fund to finance the budget. From January to October, Russia's gold holdings declined for ten consecutive months, decreasing by approximately 72 tons.

Compared to other sellers, Russia's reduction is more sustained. Turkey mainly faces financial pressure from exchange rates and energy imports, while Azerbaijan rebalances its gold holdings after exceeding the portfolio limit. Russia's gold sales directly serve fiscal financing needs and are not a one-off portfolio adjustment.

Azerbaijan's reduction is closer to a one-off portfolio rebalancing. The country's National Petroleum Fund sold 21.9 tons of gold in the first quarter, mainly because rising gold prices pushed up its holdings, exceeding the portfolio limit.

For the next six months, gold holdings remained at 178.1 tons. Turkey net sold approximately 70 tons of gold in the first quarter, with the reduction mainly concentrated in March. At that time, rising energy import bills and financial pressure to defend the lira's exchange rate led the central bank to use an additional 80 tons of gold for gold-foreign exchange swaps. Turkish Central Bank Governor Fatih Karahan stated that the gold in the swap transactions would return to reserves upon maturity. By June, the outstanding swap balance had decreased to approximately 60 tons, with net direct sales of only 4 tons in the second quarter. This indicates that Turkey's gold reduction was primarily a concentrated operation in March, rather than a sustained large-scale sell-off. Saudi Arabia: Dollar Demand Sparks Market Speculation Saudi Arabia is also under scrutiny due to fiscal and dollar liquidity pressures. Third-quarter oil revenues fell 23% year-on-year, and Riyadh recorded a deficit of 84.3 billion riyals, while simultaneously needing to maintain the riyal's peg to the dollar. On the other hand, Saudi Aramco's revenue and other sales-related income rose from $111.5 billion to $140.5 billion, and free cash flow also increased. In October, Bloomberg reported that Saudi Aramco was negotiating a $10 billion revolving credit facility to address potential funding needs arising from shipment disruptions, due to the threat of attacks by the Houthis. The market is also watching whether Saudi Arabia is raising dollars by selling gold or US Treasury bonds. US data shows that net sales of US Treasury bonds attributable to Saudi investors reached $18.7 billion in March and April, but this includes private accounts, making it impossible to determine the central bank's share. Saudi Arabia's official gold reserves stood at 323.1 tons as of August. At $3,558 per ounce, raising $10 billion through gold sales would require selling approximately 87 tons. Currently, neither the Saudi Central Bank nor the Public Investment Fund has disclosed such transactions, and there is no evidence that Saudi Arabia is selling gold on a large scale. Qatar and the UAE also reported slight declines in their gold holdings in the third quarter. Qatar Energy estimates that it will take three to five years to repair damaged facilities and restore 17% of LNG export capacity. However, Qatar's gold holdings remained unchanged from August to October, so this cannot be used to conclude that it is continuously selling off its assets.

Tether: Cooling Buying is More Worth Noting than Selling Off

Tether's changes in gold holdings do not support the claim of a large-scale sell-off. In September, its USDT reserves corresponding to gold vaults decreased by 3.4 tons compared to June, but XAUT token vaults increased by 3.7 tons during the same period, with the combined holdings rising slightly from 168.2 tons to 168.5 tons.

These two types of vaults correspond to USDT reserves and customer-held gold tokens, respectively. The combined statistics are to measure the total physical gold demand of related projects and do not include Tether's own gold investments.

However, Tether's pace of acquisition has indeed slowed significantly. Its filings show that, after accounting for changes in asset value, the company suffered a loss of $4.21 billion in the second quarter. From buying 14 tons of gold in a single quarter to almost ceasing acquisitions recently, Tether's cooling buying activity means that gold has lost an important source of marginal demand.

data.title: How can Hong Kong or Singapore platforms serving EU users determine their DAC8 obligations?
data.description:
Key Takeaways

The applicability of DAC8 to non-EU platforms depends on whether they provide crypto-asset services involving reportable users and whether they have access points as required by EU member states. Having only EU users does not automatically create a reporting obligation.

Group headquarters, client contracting entities, actual service providers, and transaction execution entities may belong to different legal entities. Companies need to clarify service relationships, authorization status, and reporting responsibilities by entity.

Whether a user is a reportable user is primarily determined based on tax residency and due diligence results. IP address, nationality, and account registration location can only serve as clues for verification.

Hong Kong and Singapore have completed local CARF legislation, and the relevant rules will be implemented from 2027. Local CARF reporting, MCAA information exchange, and DAC8 equivalent exemptions remain different levels of legal judgment.

Introduction

In November 2026, Hong Kong's "Taxation (Amendment) (Crypto Asset Reporting Framework and Revised Common Reporting Standard) Ordinance 2026" was officially gazetted, and Hong Kong's CARF rules are scheduled to be implemented from January 1, 2027. Singapore also published its CARF implementation regulations in August 2026, confirming that they will take effect from January 1, 2027. Both jurisdictions plan to start exchanging tax information on crypto asset transactions with relevant partner jurisdictions from 2028.

For crypto asset platforms headquartered in Hong Kong or Singapore that provide services to global users through websites and mobile applications, local CARF implementation is now in the preparation stage. Meanwhile, the EU's DAC8 will be applicable from January 1, 2026, and data collection for the first reporting year has begun.

If a company registers and obtains a local license in Hong Kong or Singapore, does that mean it doesn't need to consider DAC8? If a group has EU users, does it need to register and report in the EU? Can the local CARF meet the equivalent reporting requirements of DAC8? These questions need to be assessed in conjunction with the services actually provided by the company, the group's legal entity arrangements, the tax residency status of EU users, and the information exchange arrangements between non-EU jurisdictions and relevant member states. The location of the group's headquarters only indicates part of the company's business connections and cannot solely determine its tax information reporting responsibility in the EU. I. Identifying the Reporting Entity from Service Activities DAC8 applies reporting obligations to Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Providers (RCASPs). According to Annex VI Section IV, RCASPs include two types of entities: one is a Crypto-Asset Service Provider (CASP) that provides services authorized or permitted by a member country under MiCA; the other is a Crypto-Asset Operator that meets the DAC8 definition. Both types of entities must meet the relevant service and transaction conditions, namely, providing crypto-asset services that facilitate exchange transactions for or on behalf of reportable users. 1. Determining whether a platform facilitates reportable transactions. The name a platform uses externally, such as an exchange, wallet service provider, brokerage, or digital asset management platform, does not directly determine its DAC8 status. Businesses need to verify whether the services they actually provide involve relevant crypto-asset transactions, including exchanges between crypto-assets and fiat currencies, exchanges between different related crypto-assets, and other transactions that comply with regulations. DAC8's definition of Crypto-Asset Services references MiCA and explicitly includes staking and lending services; however, whether a service makes a company an RCASP still depends on whether it facilitates relevant exchange transactions for reportable users. Affiliated companies that only provide technical development or general ancillary services do not automatically become reporting entities simply because they participate in the group's business. For example, a Singaporean platform might offer spot trading, stablecoin exchange, asset custody, and staking services. Spot trading and stablecoin exchange directly involve asset exchange, and the platform needs to identify the legal entities facilitating the transactions and their customer relationships. Custody and staking services should be assessed based on specific service arrangements, related transactions, and the DAC8 definition; not all services can be included in the reporting scope simply based on the product name. 2. Separate Judgment of MiCA Market Access and DAC8 Reporting MiCA regulates market access and operational requirements for companies providing crypto asset services in the EU, while DAC8 regulates tax due diligence and information reporting for qualified service providers. The reverse solicitation exception under MiCA Article 61 is subject to authorization judgment for third-country companies. ESMA interprets this exception strictly; a company, its affiliates, or a third party acting on its behalf actively marketing or soliciting services from EU customers cannot generally be considered a reverse solicitation based solely on contractual statements. The MiCA transition period ended on July 1, 2026, and unauthorized CASPs must cease their relevant EU operations in an orderly manner as required by ESMA. The reverse solicitation exception does not constitute a separate exemption from DAC8. Enterprises should determine whether they can provide services to EU clients in accordance with MiCA and whether they meet the requirements of DAC8 regarding reporting entities and connection points.

II. Confirming Reporting Responsibilities along the Group Structure

Cross-border crypto asset platforms typically adopt a multi-entity operating structure. The group holding company is responsible for strategic management, the Hong Kong or Singapore company is responsible for client signing and daily operations, other affiliated companies are responsible for custody, technology development or transaction execution, and some EU markets are provided by local subsidiaries or branches. When determining DAC8 obligations, it is necessary to focus on specific legal entities to confirm who establishes service relationships with clients, who actually provides services, and who facilitates related transactions.

1. Verifying EU Authorized Entities and Non-EU Operating Entities

If the group has a CASP in the EU that is authorized by MiCA or authorized to provide services, this entity belongs to the entity type specified in DAC8 Section 1 A(1) and needs to identify reporting obligations based on its actual services and client transactions. The existence of a MiCA-authorized entity within a group does not automatically extend that authorization to all affiliated companies. For Crypto-Asset Operators that are not MiCA-authorized or authorized to provide services in the EU, DAC8 Section IA(2) specifies four types of connection points: The enterprise or individual is a tax resident of a Member State; the enterprise is incorporated or organized under the laws of that Member State and has legal personality or relevant reporting obligations; the enterprise is governed by that Member State; or the enterprise or individual has a habitual place of business in that Member State. Non-EU operating entities need to consider these connection points to determine whether they have reporting and due diligence obligations in a Member State.

DAC8 Connector PointFacts the Enterprise Needs to Verify
Tax Residency StatusPlace of businessWhether an entity or individual has a place of business in a particular EU member state.

The existence of EU users is not itself one of the four types of connection points mentioned above. Suppose a Hong Kong stock exchange accepts registrations from users in France and Germany through a global website, and the customer agreement, management team, and actual operations are all undertaken by a Hong Kong entity, and this entity has no branches or other legal connection points in the EU. The mere fact that a user resides in France or Germany is not sufficient to directly determine that the Hong Kong entity needs to register under DAC8.

Whether an entity or individual has a place of business in a particular EU member state.

The existence of EU users is not itself one of the four types of connection points mentioned above.

2. Separate Verification of EU Branches Branches are a separate matter. DAC8 Annex VI Section I B stipulates that when a reporting service provider facilitates a transaction through a branch located in a Member State, it must fulfill local reporting and due diligence requirements for that transaction. Branches differ legally from independent subsidiaries: the former are subject to branch rules, while the latter must identify reporting responsibilities based on their service activities, authorization status, and connection points. For eligible Crypto-Asset Operators, DAC8 also establishes a single EU registration mechanism. Companies need to determine their Member State of Registration based on the relevant connection points and complete registration according to that country's requirements. Group structure diagrams only illustrate legal relationships; companies should also map customer agreements, product services, personnel arrangements, transaction execution, and asset custody to specific entities to create a verifiable entity identification record.

III. Differentiating EU Users from Reportable Users

After confirming that the company is a reporting entity under DAC8, it is also necessary to identify which customers are reportable users. Generally, reportable users are individuals or entities identified through due diligence as tax residents of EU member states; for eligible entity customers, it is also necessary to determine whether their controllers are reportable persons. This determination is based on tax residency status, not the country of account registration or the country where the user accesses the platform.

1. Identifying Users Through Tax Residency Declarations

Suppose a Singapore exchange discovers that a large number of users on its platform have registered IP addresses from France, Germany, and Spain. This information can serve as a clue for verifying customer information, but it cannot directly prove that the user is a tax resident of the relevant country. A user who resides in Singapore long-term may access the platform through a French network; a user who registers an account in Germany may also be a tax resident of another country.

Businesses need to obtain a tax residency self-certification and verify its reasonableness in conjunction with existing customer due diligence data. The self-certification for individual users should cover information such as name, address, tax residency jurisdiction, corresponding TIN, and date of birth. For entity users, it is also necessary to determine whether they are excluded persons or active entities; for other entities, the controlling person needs to be identified and determined whether the controlling person is a reportable person. Businesses should correlate customer declarations with KYC/CDD data and handle inconsistencies between tax residency information and existing identity data. 2. Differentiating Due Diligence Timelines for Existing and New Users For users with newly established customer relationships, reporting service providers should obtain a self-certification at the time of relationship establishment. For existing individual and entity users, DAC8 requires obtaining the relevant declaration by January 1, 2027, and verifying its reasonableness based on existing data. If a company discovers changes in a customer's circumstances that render the original declaration incorrect or unreliable, it should obtain a valid new declaration or retain reasonable explanations and appropriate supporting documentation to explain the validity of the original declaration. This means that the existing KYC process needs to be aligned with tax due diligence requirements. Existing identity information, proof of address, and entity controller information can be used for verification, but companies still need to confirm whether they cover the tax residency information required by DAC8. For customers using different accounts in multiple regions, it should also be ensured that the user's identity, tax residency declaration, and the actual service provider correspond to each other. IV. Verifying the Applicability of CARF Equivalence Arrangements For platforms that have already established CARF reporting systems in Hong Kong or Singapore, it is necessary to further determine whether the local reporting arrangements meet the DAC8 equivalence requirements. DAC8 Annex VI establishes concepts such as Qualified Non-Union Jurisdiction and Effective Qualifying Competent Authority Agreement (EMA). These mechanisms allow qualified reporting service providers to avoid duplication of some due diligence and reporting obligations in EU and non-EU jurisdictions, provided they meet statutory conditions. 1. CARF Local Legislation Does Not Equate to Automatic DAC8 Exemption Suppose a Singaporean platform has established a client due diligence and annual reporting process under CARF Regulations 2026 and plans to submit reports to IRAS. The platform still needs to verify whether it meets the applicable conditions of the DAC8 equivalent mechanism and whether a valid EMA exists between Singapore and the relevant EU member states. CARF local registration, MCAA signing, and DAC8 exemption are different legal statuses and cannot be substituted for each other. DAC8 sets conditions for duplicate due diligence and reporting at the reporting service provider level, as well as duplicate reporting of user information that should be reported. Companies need to confirm whether the relevant non-EU jurisdiction falls under the DAC8 definition of Qualified Non-Union Jurisdiction, whether the information exchange agreement is valid, whether the reported information meets the corresponding requirements, and whether the company has already completed the relevant reporting in that jurisdiction. 2. Verify Information Exchange Agreements and Reporting Years According to DAC8 Annex VI Section IV, Qualified Non-Union Jurisdiction refers to non-EU jurisdictions that have valid qualified competent authority agreements with all member states listed in their published list of reportable jurisdictions. DAC8 Article 8ad also stipulates that, where the OECD CARF is determined to be the minimum standard or an equivalent standard, relevant information can be considered to meet the corresponding information requirements, but a competent authority agreement between the relevant member state and the non-EU jurisdiction is still required. The Irish Revenue Service's list of CARF/DAC8 reporting jurisdictions includes Hong Kong and Singapore, with the first exchange expected to begin in 2028, and the agreement type marked as MCAA. This indicates that Ireland's published CARF exchange arrangements cover both jurisdictions, but the list itself does not prove that Hong Kong or Singapore has met all the DAC8 conditions for Qualified Non-Union Jurisdiction, nor does it presume that other EU member states have established similar arrangements with either jurisdiction. Companies need to verify each item by target member state, agreement status, and reporting year. 3. CARF Implementation Progress in Hong Kong and Singapore As of November 2026, both Hong Kong and Singapore have completed their local CARF legislation processes, and the relevant rules will come into effect on January 1, 2027. Both jurisdictions plan to begin their first information exchange with their partner jurisdictions in 2028, but domestic reporting arrangements and technical requirements should still be confirmed in accordance with the latest guidelines from the local authorities. < ... The first international exchange is planned to begin in 2028. The program is scheduled to start in September 2028.
Verification itemsHong KongSingapore
Implementation DateJanuary 1, 2027.January 1, 2027.January 1, 2027.
Competent AuthorityHong Kong Inland Revenue Department (IRD).Singapore Inland Revenue Authority (IRAS).
Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS).
Follow-up VerificationPartner jurisdiction list, registration procedures, application format and technical guidelines.Partner jurisdiction list, bilateral exchange relationships, registration and annual reporting requirements.

Companies should continuously monitor the partner jurisdiction lists and exchange relationships published by both locations.

The initial exchange of local CARFs is scheduled for 2028 and does not independently demonstrate that its arrangements for the 2026 reporting year meet DAC8 equivalence requirements. For platforms serving multiple EU countries, it is also necessary to verify the relevant member state's competent authority agreements and local implementation requirements on a case-by-case basis. V. Applying Applicability Judgments to Group Operations For platforms operating in Hong Kong, Singapore, and the EU markets simultaneously, DAC8 judgments need to be applied to legal entities and actual business operations. Assume a group headquartered in Hong Kong, with a main operating company in Singapore, providing transaction services to EU users through a local website; the group also has a subsidiary in Germany authorized by MiCA. The company needs to separately confirm the service scope of the Hong Kong, Singapore, and German entities, identify which entity contracts with and serves customers, and then determine whether each entity constitutes a reporting entity under DAC8. If a German subsidiary is an authorized or permitted service provider under DAC8 Section 1 A(1), it should fulfill its reporting obligations based on its actual business operations. Singapore companies need to determine their obligations based on their own service activities, EU connections, and branch arrangements, and further verify CARF equivalence. Hong Kong parent companies should also make their own assessments based on their actual services and legal relationships. The completion of a CARF or DAC8 filing by one entity within the group does not automatically supersede other separate legal entities. Enterprises can compile applicability judgments into continuously updated internal working papers, recording at least the following: Verification Dimensions Facts Requiring Confirmation Recommended Materials for Retention Service ActivitiesWhether or not services are provided to facilitate cryptocurrency exchange transactions for users who should report them.Product list, service agreement, transaction process.Product list, service agreement, transaction process. ... Main StructureWho signs the contract, who operates, and who executes the transaction; whether there is an EU-authorized entity or branch.Group structure diagram, explanation of main entity relationships, authorization documents.Group structure diagram, explanation of main entity relationships, authorization documents.< ... EU UsersUser's tax residency status, entity customers, and controlling person information.Self-declaration, KYC/CDD information, user ownership records. Equivalent ArrangementsAgreement validity, information correspondence, reporting completion status, and applicable year.Domestic regulations, list of competent authorities, exchange agreements, and filing records.

When the Group adds new EU business, establishes local subsidiaries, adjusts the contracting parties of clients, or changes transaction execution arrangements, the original DAC8 judgment may change accordingly.

Companies should update their entity relationships, reporting connections, and information exchange arrangements in a synchronized manner, and incorporate the findings into customer due diligence, data collection, and reporting processes.

Conclusion

For crypto asset platforms headquartered in Hong Kong or Singapore and operating in the EU market, DAC8 applicability assessment involves service activities, legal entities, user tax residency, and cross-border information exchange arrangements. Companies need to first identify the entities actually providing services, then verify their legal connections with EU member states, subsequently identify reportable users, and determine whether the local CARF meets the DAC8 equivalent reporting requirements.

The Hong Kong and Singapore CARFs will be implemented in 2027. Companies can integrate local customer due diligence, transaction data collection, and annual reporting preparation into their existing compliance systems. Simultaneously, the group needs to separately maintain EU legal entities, branches, and related reporting responsibilities, verifying effective exchange arrangements by target member state and reporting year.

For platforms operating across borders, the ability to correlate specific legal entities, service activities, customer tax residency, and reporting jurisdictions is fundamental for conducting tax due diligence and preparing tax returns. Companies should incorporate this assessment into their business launch, entity restructuring, and annual compliance review processes. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) 1. Do cryptocurrency exchanges headquartered in Hong Kong or Singapore necessarily need to fulfill DAC8 obligations when serving EU users? Not necessarily. Companies need to consider their actual service activities, MiCA authorization status, and the connection points specified in DAC8 Annex VI Section I. The existence of EU users does not automatically constitute a reporting connection point for non-EU Crypto-Asset Operators. 2. If CARF registration has already been completed in Hong Kong or Singapore, is it still necessary to assess DAC8 compliance?

Required. CARF local registration and reporting do not automatically replace DAC8 obligations. Companies also need to verify the existence of a valid competent authority agreement between their locality and the relevant EU member state, and confirm the correspondence of information, reporting completion status, and applicable year.

3. Can a MiCA customer's initiative to initiate a service exception exempt them from DAC8 reporting obligations?

No. The exception in MiCA Article 61 involves market access requirements for third-country companies. DAC8 has separate reporting entities, connection points, and rules for exemption from duplicate reporting, which companies need to determine separately.
